stories.title: Hanwha Construction Joins South Korean Project to Boost AI Data Center Efficiency
stories.summary: Hanwha Construction has joined a South Korean government-backed project aimed at improving AI data center energy efficiency. The initiative focuses on construction and engineering approaches to reduce power consumption in next-generation facilities.
stories.why_it_matters: Bringing a major construction group into a state-led efficiency program signals Korea is treating data center energy performance as industrial policy, not just an operator concern. Contractors that master efficient AI-facility design stand to gain an edge as power constraints make efficiency a permitting and cost differentiator.

stories.title: OCP APAC Summit Highlights AI Data Center Management as Power Constraints Grow
stories.summary: The Open Compute Project's APAC Summit focused on managing AI data centers amid growing power constraints, TechRepublic reports. Discussions covered operational efficiency, liquid cooling, and grid-aware workload management.
stories.why_it_matters: The agenda shift from capacity expansion to operational efficiency reflects the industry's acknowledgment that power availability, not capital or land, is now the binding constraint across APAC. Operators that adopt OCP-style efficiency practices earliest will be best positioned to win allocations in power-rationed markets like Singapore and Tokyo.
stories.content:
The Open Compute Project’s APAC Summit opened in Taipei on Aug. 11 with AI-scale systems management, power, cooling, and server architecture in focus as increasingly dense AI infrastructure changes how data center operators manage hardware at scale.

OCP’s Scalable Cloud Infrastructure Management work targets hardware-management problems in facilities with 100,000 nodes or more. Across Asia-Pacific, that push toward fleet-scale management is unfolding as operators simultaneously contend with rapid capacity growth, denser racks, and tighter access to power.

## **OCP scales hardware management for AI**

OCP’s Scalable Cloud Infrastructure Management, or SCIM, subproject examines how hardware-management data can move across large data center networks and how technologies such as AI and machine learning systems, RDMA, PCIe/CXL, and DDR affect fleet operations. OCP’s SCIM is unrelated to the identity-provisioning standard that uses the same acronym.

The 2026 OCP APAC Summit extends that work across AI infrastructure, including telemetry and management systems that connect facility operations with equipment in the data hall. As GPU clusters expand, networking has become another AI infrastructure constraint, increasing the need for visibility beyond compute hardware alone.

Regional growth adds pressure. Asia-Pacific’s data center development pipeline increased by 7,103 MW in the first half of 2026 to 26,455 MW, according to Cushman & Wakefield. Vacancy fell from 10.9% to 10.3% despite new supply entering the market. In Indonesia, Firmus is planning a 360 MW Nvidia-powered AI data center on Batam, with initial operations targeted for 2027.

GEICO provides an enterprise example of the operational work involved in open infrastructure. The insurer reported cutting compute cost per core by more than 50% and storage cost per gigabyte by more than 60% after deploying OCP hardware across two colocation facilities with more than 1,000 servers, according to its OCP adoption white paper.

The deployment also required new processes and skills for firmware, validation, inventory, and fleet lifecycle management. GEICO’s results are not a regional benchmark, but its experience shows that lower hardware costs can come with higher requirements for in-house infrastructure engineering.

## **Power constraints reshape APAC deployments**

Power availability is increasingly shaping where new capacity can be built. Schneider Electric executive Jean-Christophe Moureau told Computer Weekly in May 2026 that Singapore faced energy constraints on additional data center development through 2028.

Higher-density AI systems compound the problem. AlixPartners says operators may need to plan for rack densities around 135 kW for AI workloads, compared with 15–30 kW for typical cloud deployments. The shift is also making liquid cooling increasingly central to AI infrastructure as operators contend with greater heat loads.

A Feb. 10, 2026, Deloitte report recommends shifting suitable workloads across time or location when energy conditions allow and incorporating storage and operational flexibility into data center design.

Rising rack density is bringing server, network, cooling, and power management closer together. OCP’s standards work is aimed at making those increasingly interconnected systems easier to operate as AI deployments grow larger.

**Read more: Australia is confronting a similar infrastructure challenge as** **rapid AI data center growth puts new pressure on the power grid****.**

stories.title: Australia's CDC Considers New Data Center in New Zealand
stories.summary: Australian data center operator CDC is considering building a new facility in New Zealand, Data Center Dynamics reports. The move would extend CDC's government-grade infrastructure footprint beyond Australia and Canberra.
stories.why_it_matters: A CDC entry would bring a security-cleared, sovereign-capable operator into New Zealand's small but growing market, raising the competitive bar for incumbent providers. It also reflects trans-Tasman governments' shared interest in allied-nation data infrastructure resilience.
stories.content:
Australian data center firm CDC has announced interest in a potential data center in New Zealand in partnership with Contact Energy.

The site would be on the country's North Island in Stratford, Taranaki, based on land near Contact Energy’s former Taranaki Combined Cycle power station.

![New Zealand.JPG](https://media.datacenterdynamics.com/media/images/New_Zealand.width-358.jpg) 

CDC said the site has existing energy and connectivity infrastructure, including high-capacity fiber, both terrestrial and subsea, offering connection to Auckland, the location of New Zealand’s international cables.

The potential facility would be focused on supporting critical and sovereign workloads in government and public sector systems, healthcare and emergency services, scientific and research computing, banking and payments, and emergency and critical communications networks.

Electricity to the facility would be supplied under a long-term contract and supported by Contact Energy’s renewable development pipeline. CDC’s other New Zealand data centers are powered by 100 percent renewable energy.

The facility will also feature a closed-loop cooling system, which CDC currently uses in its other facilities.

CDC said the project remains at “exploration stage” and any development will be subject to due diligence, consenting, and commercial requirements.

"CDC builds the infrastructure that governments, health systems, emergency services, researchers and financial institutions depend on. This is where sovereign data is held, where critical systems stay online, and where the most sensitive information stays in country," said CDC founder and chief executive Greg Boorer. "Stratford has the potential to bring together renewable generation, grid connection, fiber and a skilled technical workforce in a way very few places can. That combination is why we are looking at it seriously."

Last week, CDC announced plans to develop a new campus in Sydney.

Founded in 2007, Infratil-backed CDC has nearly 20 sites in operation and development across Sydney, Canberra, Melbourne, and Auckland, New Zealand.

The company currently has more than 600MW of data center capacity in operation and development across Melbourne, Sydney, Canberra, and New Zealand. It has a future development pipeline of a further 1.6GW to 2034.

stories.title: Japan's Akita AI Data Center Now Estimated at $12.6 Billion
stories.summary: The estimated cost of a planned AI data center project in Akita, Japan, has risen to approximately US$12.6 billion, according to TechRepublic. The figure marks a significant increase from earlier projections for the development.
stories.why_it_matters: The ballooning estimate illustrates how power procurement, construction costs, and GPU-era facility requirements are inflating Japanese mega-project budgets, testing the economics of large-scale builds outside Tokyo and Osaka. For regional governments courting such projects, it raises the stakes on promised power and subsidy commitments.
stories.content:
Japan could gain one of its largest AI data centers under a project in Akita now expected to cost more than ¥2 trillion, or roughly $12.6 billion, with Abu Dhabi sovereign investor Mubadala considering an investment.

If completed, the 300–500 MW project would add substantial AI compute capacity outside Japan’s established data center hubs.

For enterprises planning future Japan-based workloads, however, the useful capacity will depend on whether organizers can secure financing, grid connections, and enough deliverable power to support the proposed scale.

## A ¥2 trillion project could expand Japan’s AI capacity map

Japan Today reported that expected construction costs now exceed ¥2 trillion and that Mubadala Investment Co. is considering backing the project. No final investment commitment has been announced.

The financial scope being discussed is considerably larger than earlier figures. JETRO reported in November 2025 that planned investment could reach ¥400 billion.

The figures are not directly comparable because the earlier number described expected investment while the new figure is reported as construction cost. Still, the latest estimate establishes Akita as a much larger infrastructure project than its initial public outline suggested.

Akita City signed a cooperation agreement with S2 and Bitgrit in October 2025. Organizers say they have secured 50 hectares in a renewable-energy industrial park in northern Akita City and are targeting full operation around 2033.

That scale could broaden where enterprises source Japan-based AI infrastructure. Most current capacity remains concentrated around established markets, although providers are expanding, including Alibaba Cloud with its fifth Japan data center.

Akita would offer a different proposition: large-scale AI infrastructure built around access to regional renewable generation rather than proximity to an existing metropolitan data center cluster.

## Power and financing will decide how much capacity arrives

The project’s official site describes 300–500 MW of renewable-energy potential, including offshore wind. That does not mean the data center has already secured 500 MW of usable IT load or the grid connections required to deliver it.

That distinction directly affects future customers. A planned 500 MW campus does not create 500 MW of bookable compute capacity if electricity connections, substations, or generation cannot arrive on the same timetable.

Similar constraints are already affecting data center expansion elsewhere. US grid capacity constraints are slowing some proposed projects, while Australia is preparing for additional pressure from AI data center demand.

Akita therefore remains a long-term capacity prospect rather than infrastructure enterprises can include in near-term deployment plans. A Mubadala investment could strengthen the financing side, but customers will also need evidence of grid interconnection, construction milestones, operating partners, and committed capacity before the project becomes a realistic sourcing option.

**Also read:** **Uptime Institute found 57% of major data center outages now cost more than $100,000, even as overall outage frequency declines.**

stories.title: Malaysian Property Giant Sells 36-Acre Cyberjaya Land Parcel for Data Center Development
stories.summary: A major Malaysian property developer has sold a 36-acre land parcel in Cyberjaya for data center development, Data Center Dynamics reports. The transaction adds to a wave of land deals in Malaysia's established tech corridor.
stories.why_it_matters: The deal confirms Cyberjaya remains a live data center market even as developer attention shifts to Johor, giving buyers a power-and-fiber-ready alternative in the Klang Valley. For Malaysian conglomerates monetizing land banks, it demonstrates that data center demand continues to set the floor for industrial land values.
stories.content:
The subsidiary of Malaysian property giant Malaysian Resources Corporation Berhad (MRCB) is selling a 36-acre land parcel in Cyberjaya for potential data center development.

MRCB announced on Friday, August 7, that it had entered into a conditional sale and purchase agreement with Digital Cosmos, under which MRCB would sell seven parcels of land for RM419 million ($102m).

![MRCB Logo](https://media.datacenterdynamics.com/media/images/MRCB_Logo.width-358.jpg) 

Digital Cosmos was incorporated in Malaysia just three months ago. The company is a subsidiary of Digital Cosmos (S) Pte Ltd, which was incorporated in Singapore in June.

MRCB’s filing with Malaysia’s bourse states that the company is “principally involved in the development and operation of data centers.” It is unclear whether the company has previously developed data centers.

The agreement also states that Digital Cosmos will be responsible for getting written approval for the provision of 182MW worth of power and at least 9.41 million liters per day of water for the data center.

Cyberjaya is a planned tech city located on the outskirts of Malaysia’s capital, Kuala Lumpur.

stories.title: NTT-Backed Consortium Targets Ishikari as Japan Data Center Hub
stories.summary: A consortium backed by NTT is targeting Ishikari, Hokkaido, for development as a major data center hub, according to Telecom Review Asia. The initiative seeks to leverage the region's cool climate and available land and power.
stories.why_it_matters: The push aligns with Japan's policy of decentralizing digital infrastructure away from earthquake-exposed Tokyo, and Hokkaido's cold climate and renewable potential make it one of the few places in Japan that can host large AI campuses. Success would redistribute investment and grid planning to northern Japan while intensifying competition among regional hubs.
stories.content:
NTT East Corporation has joined a consortium of data center, telecommunications, energy, and infrastructure companies seeking to develop Ishikari City in Hokkaido into a major data center cluster.

The Ishikari Data Center Consortium will focus on strengthening the infrastructure needed to support data center development, including power and telecommunications networks. The group will also work with local authorities to establish incentives and other measures to support further development.

The consortium includes Sakura Internet, Kyocera, Tokyu Land Corporation, Ishikari Renewable Energy Data Center No. 1 LLC, Flower Communications, Broadband Tower Inc., NTT ME Corporation, Ishikari Regional Energy LLC, Liene Inc., and Hokkaido Integrated Communications Network Co., Ltd., also known as HotNet.

**Latest:** NTT Launches 200-MW Data Center Campus in Chiba, Japan

Ishikari, located in Hokkaido’s Ishikari Subprefecture, is emerging as a data center location, with the Ishikari Bay New Port area offering access to renewable energy resources and relatively low disaster risks. The consortium aims to promote Ishikari as a domestic data center hub and one of Japan’s leading data center clusters.

NTT East said the consortium will work to ensure that residents and local businesses experience the social value of data center development while promoting Ishikari as a data center cluster nationwide.

Sakura Internet has operated its data center in Ishikari since 2011. The company has expanded the site and has been deploying GPUs there.

Tokyu Land, Flower Communications, and Broadband Tower partnered on a 15-MW data center project in Ishikari in 2024. The project is due to launch in 2026.

The initiative adds to Hokkaido’s data center footprint. Data Center Map lists nine data centers on the island, centered around Sapporo. Operators with data centers in Hokkaido include SoftBank, Kyocera, HotNet, Sakura Internet, KDDI, and Rakuten.

Eurus Energy is also developing a wind-powered data center project in Wakkanai, northern Hokkaido.

NTT East provides services from around 30 data center locations in Japan, including facilities in Tokyo, Yokohama, Chiba, Saitama, Ibaraki, Tochigi, and Gunma. NTT’s telecommunications businesses also include NTT West, NTT DOCOMO, and NTT Communications.

The Ishikari consortium brings together companies involved in the city’s data center, energy, and communications infrastructure. By strengthening the infrastructure needed for data center operations and coordinating with local government, the group aims to support further development and establish Ishikari as a larger data center hub in Japan.
